docComment.comment: A `§§` block documents whatever is declared below it, where a `§` block stays a private note. The tags, Parameter names and code spans are what make the two read differently even in a theme that colours every comment alike. `\G` anchors a tag to the head of the line, exactly as the Compiler's own grammar does, so an `@param` written in prose stays prose.
docComment.name: comment.block.documentation.essence

patterns.comment: A `@param` naming nothing documents nothing and is left in the prose by the Compiler, so it is left unlit here too. The em-dash is what the Compiler requires between a tag and its text, so it reads as the separator it is rather than as prose.

`@example` carries no text on its own line — its assertions are written on the lines below it, and the Compiler compiles and runs them as tests of their own. So there is no separator to scope beside the tag, which is the whole of what tells this rule from the two above it.

comment.comment: The `(?!§)` keeps a Documentation block out of here on its own, so that the order of the two rules is not what tells them apart.
comment.name: comment.line.essence

moduleSection.comment: All four of `import`, `export`, `from` and `as` stay valid Identifiers everywhere else — `from` is an Argument label in the standard library — so none of them can be lit on the word alone. The block is what scopes them: it opens at the very start of a line with a brace and holds nothing but groups and names, so `from` and `as` inside it are always the Keywords. The block ends at a brace written at the very start of a line, because the groups inside it close on indented braces of their own. Semantic Tokens correct whatever is left.

string.comment: A String legitimately spans lines, so running on past the end of the line is the correct reading of an unterminated quote rather than a bug. A '{ … }' hole re-enters the language so its Expression is highlighted as code.
string.name: string.quoted.double.essence

controlKeyword.comment: `define` is a reserved Keyword, so it lights on the word alone. `otherwise` is a valid Identifier — as `case` and `with` on this list already are — and is lit here anyway for the same reason they are: telling an arm's terminator from a name spelled the same would need to know what block the line stands in, which a grammar of regexes can not see, and the word all but always ends an arm where it is written. An editor that asks for Semantic Tokens recolours a name spelled that way anyway, because those are read off what an Identifier resolves to. The third word an arm is written with, `as`, is not here — it is scoped under the contextual rules below.
controlKeyword.name: keyword.control.essence

contextualKeyword.comment: The words that are Keywords in one place and ordinary Identifiers everywhere else. None of them can be lit on the word alone, so each rule here is what scopes its own.

patterns.comment: `is` is also a Method name — `@::is(other)` — and `where` is also an Argument label — `everyItem(where check:)` — so neither can be lit on the word alone. What follows decides: a conformance bound and a Match guard are followed by a Type or by `@`, a call and a label never are. That reading answers a `where` wherever it stands, line breaks included, which is why it keeps the word as well as the two rules below.
patterns.name: keyword.other.essence

patterns.comment: The `where` the rule above can not reach: a Guard whose Condition is an ordinary Expression — `case { x, y } where x::is(y)`, `case 0 where count::isNot(1)` — which begins with a lowercase name as often as not, and so says nothing about itself. What stands in FRONT of it is what tells a Guard from the Argument LABEL spelled the same: a label opens its Argument, so a `(`, a comma or the head of the line precedes it, where a Guard follows the Matcher it guards — a Pattern's `}`, a Type's last letter, a Literal's last digit, a `_`. What may follow is where a Condition starts, and the excluded characters are what a value NAMED `where` is followed by instead: `constant where = 3` and `where::length()` both stay unlit. A `where` whose Condition is written on the NEXT line is reached by neither this rule nor the one below — this asks for the Condition behind it and that asks for the word at the head of its line — so it goes unlit, which is the side to miss on.

A Guard the Formatter broke onto a line of its own, which the rule above can never light: that one wants the Matcher immediately in front, and a line break and an indent stand there instead. The other line-initial `where` in the corpus is an Argument label in an exploded Argument list — `where check: (…) -> Boolean,` and `where (item) { … },` — and the trailing comma is what tells the two apart, exactly as it does for the `as` of an arm below: the Formatter ends every exploded Argument with one, and a Guard ends in its Condition. So a label written LAST in such a list, which carries no comma, is lit as though it were a Guard — the one shape the rule reads wrong, and a rarer one than the Guard it is here for.
The `tests { … }` section. `tests` is an ordinary Identifier everywhere else, and the Parser tells the two apart exactly the way this does: by the `{` that must follow it.
patterns.name: storage.type.essence

patterns.comment: A `test`, a `suite` or a `benchmark` opens where the String Literal naming it follows — which is the Parser's own rule, and what keeps `constant test = 5` unlit.
patterns.name: storage.type.essence

patterns.comment: `skipped "why"`, one of the Modifiers a test or a suite carries. The Modifier grammar is deliberately open — a name and the arguments behind it, with the vocabulary left to the stage that knows it — so none of these three is a reserved Keyword, and each is scoped by what follows it the way the item Keywords above are. A skip's reason is mandatory, so a String is always what follows this one.
patterns.name: storage.modifier.essence

patterns.comment: `tagged slow, network` — the bare names a run selects on. What follows is a name, so the excluded characters are what a value spelled `tagged` is followed by instead: `constant tagged = …` and `tagged::length()` both stay unlit.
patterns.name: storage.modifier.essence

patterns.comment: `focused`, which carries nothing at all — so what follows it is the item's own block. A call and an assignment are what a value spelled this way is followed by, and neither is a brace.
patterns.name: storage.modifier.essence

patterns.comment: And the same Modifier on a line of its OWN, which is where the Formatter puts one under a `test "…"` head. Nothing may stand in front of it there, because ending its line is not on its own a fact about a Modifier: `constant enabled = focused` ends one too, and a value spelled this way is not one.

`across [ … ]` opens a table test. The rows may be any Expression, but the brackets around them are the Parser's own requirement — a row is a test in its own right and has to be countable before anything runs — so the bracket is what scopes the word, and `constant across = 3` stays unlit.
patterns.name: keyword.control.essence

patterns.comment: `for any (…)` opens a property test. `for` is lit by the control Keyword rule already, so what this scopes is the `any` behind it — an ordinary Identifier everywhere else.

`expect` and `require` open an assertion where an Expression follows them. The excluded characters are what a name called `expect` is followed by instead — `constant expect = 6`, `expect::is(6)`, `f(expect)`.
patterns.name: keyword.control.essence

patterns.comment: `start` and `complete` are Keywords where an Expression follows them and ordinary Identifiers everywhere else — the Parser's own rule, and the one `expect` and `require` above are scoped by. The excluded characters are what a value called `start` is followed by instead: `constant start = 1`, `start::isAbove(0)`, `{ start = 1 }` and the shorthand `{ start }`. An Argument LABEL spelled either way — `f(start value)` — lights as though it were the Keyword, which is the one shape this reads wrong and the same one the assertion rule above lives with.
patterns.name: keyword.control.essence

patterns.comment: `matches snapshot`, and the `from "name"` that makes it one kept beside the file rather than one recorded inline. Neither word means anything alone — the PAIR is what the Parser reads — so the pair is what is matched, and the `from` is scoped with it because it belongs to this form rather than to a Module section.

`as` opens a `define` arm — `as "A" if score::isAbove(90)` — where the rule below can never light it: that one wants an Identifier character immediately in front, and an arm head has a line break and an indent there instead. An arm reads as an arm, so it is lit as one, and as control flow rather than as a binder. The grammar is regex only and can not see that this line stands inside a `define` block, so line start is what stands in for it. What may follow is where an arm's value starts, which unlike a binder's may be a String or a Case; the excluded characters are what a line beginning with a name spelled `as` is followed by instead. The whitespace turns most of those away on its own — `as::length()` and `as.member` have none — so what is left to exclude is an assignment to a name called `as`. The other line-initial `as` in the corpus is an Argument LABEL in an exploded Argument list — `normalize(` then `as NormalizationForm#DecomposedCanonical,` then `)`, which the Formatter writes itself — and the trailing comma is what tells the two apart: the Formatter ends every exploded Argument with one, and an arm ends in its Condition, in `otherwise`, or in the bracket its value carries on past. An arm broken across lines behind a comma of its own goes unlit, which is the side to miss on: an unlit Keyword reads as text, where a lit label reads as a construct that is not there.

`as` binds a Pattern's member under another name — `{ x as y }`, `{ origin as { x, y } }` — or names the whole value, `{ x, y } as point`. It is an Argument label as well, so `normalize(as #ComposedCanonical)` is a call and not a Pattern, and only what sits on BOTH sides tells the two apart: a label opens its Argument, so a `(`, a comma or the head of the line precedes it, where a binder follows what it binds — a member name, the `>` closing the Type that member was constrained to, or the Pattern's own `}`. What may follow is the Parser's own two-Token rule verbatim, a name or a nested Pattern and nothing else, which leaves `{ as }` and the trailing name of `{ as as as }` unlit as the Identifiers they are. The whitespace is matched rather than looked behind because Oniguruma looks back a fixed number of characters only. NOTE: A binder written on the line below what it binds stays unlit, and a value NAMED `as` in front of a block — `if as { … }` — lights as though it were a binder. Both need the Parser to tell, which one line read by one regex is not.

fraction.comment: The sign carries the lookbehind rather than the whole Literal: `<-5` returns a five, and reading the `-` of `<-` as its sign would leave the digit unlit.
fraction.name: constant.numeric.fraction.essence

decimal.comment: Digits on both sides of the dot, which is what keeps `1.foo` an Integer and a member path; the rule comes before `number` so that a decimal is lit whole rather than as an Integer that stops at the dot.
decimal.name: constant.numeric.decimal.essence

wildcard.comment: What follows is what separates the wildcard from the `__` a native invocation opens with, which is never followed by any of these.
wildcard.name: variable.language.wildcard.essence

property.comment: Ahead of `type`, because a member is not a Type however it is spelled — `Number.PI` names a member of `Number`. The `(?!\()` is what leaves a CALLED member to `functionInvocation`; ordering alone can not do it, since both rules would start at the same character. The quantifier is possessive so that the name can not give a character back to satisfy that lookahead — `.forCrowd(` would otherwise match `forCrow` and leave the `d` behind.
property.name: variable.other.property.essence

type.comment: Ahead of `functionInvocation`, so that `Foo(` reads as the Type it names rather than as a Function — both start at the same character, and the earlier rule wins that tie. A lowercase call is untouched, since this rule needs a capital.
type.name: entity.name.type.essence

patterns.comment: The language's only return form, which is control flow rather than arithmetic.
patterns.name: keyword.control.return.essence

punctuation.comment: Essence has no comparison Operators, so an angle bracket the Operator and Method rules above have left alone is unambiguously a Type Parameter's.
